Systolic geometry of translation surfaces
Tobias Columbus, Frank Herrlich, Bjoern Muetzel and Gabriela Weitze-Schmithüsen
Abstract
In this paper we investigate the systolic landscape of translation surfaces for ﬁxed genus and ﬁxed
angles of their cone points. We furthermore study how the systoles of a translation surface relate to
the systoles of its graph of saddle connections. This allows us to develop an algorithm to compute
the systolic ratio of origamis in the stratum (1, 1). We compute the maximal systolic ratio of all
origamis in (1, 1) with up to 67 squares. These computations support a conjecture of Judge and
Parlier about the maximal systolic ratio in (1, 1).
Keywords: translation surfaces, systoles, maximal surfaces.
Mathematics Subject Classiﬁcation (2010): 30F10, 32G15 and 53C22.

We present an algorithm to compute the systoles of the graph of saddle connections of a given origami
surface (cf. Algorithm I and II). We use this in order to compute the maximal systolic ratio of all origamis
with at most 67 squares in (1, 1) (cf. Section 5). These computations support Conjecture 1.2 of Judge
and Parlier in [JP].
This article is structured in the following way. After introducing the necessary tools and deﬁnitions
in Section 2 we present the results about short geodesics on translation surfaces. Then we provide an
interesting property of maximal surfaces in Section 3. In Section 4, we introduce the graph of saddle
connections and clarify how its systoles relate to the systoles of the translation surface. Finally, in Section
5 we present the algorithm to compute the length of a systole of the graph of saddle connections for an
origami surface.

A crucial role in the understanding of translation surfaces is played by origamis or square-tiled surfaces
(cf. e.g. [DGZZ], [GM], [HS], [HL], [MMY], [MYZ]). We brieﬂy summarize some relevant facts about
origamis which are needed for this article. You can ﬁnd a more elaborate introduction in [Sci2]. Origamis
are translation surfaces deﬁned by gluing together ﬁnitely many copies of Euclidean unit squares along
the upper and lower or the right and left edges. An origami 푂is the collection of the corresponding
gluing data. It is entirely determined by two permutations 휎푎and 휎푏in 푆푑, where 푑is the number of
squares, 휎푎describes the horizontal gluings and 휎푏describes the vertical gluings. More precisely we
label the squares by 1, . . . , 푑. The right edge of the square with label 푖is glued by a translation with
the left edge of the square with label 휎푎(푖). Similarly, the upper edge of the square with label 푖is glued
by a translation with the lower edge of the square with label 휎푏(푖). Renumbering the squares leads to
simultaneous conjugation of the pair (휎푎, 휎푏). The resulting surface 푆is then tessellated by squares and
naturally carries a translation structure (see Figure 7). A more detailed explanation of how to describe
origamis in different combinatorial ways can be found in Section 2 of [Sci1]. The group SL(2, ℤ) acts on
the set of origamis: For 퐴∈SL(2, ℤ) and an origami 푂we apply the afﬁne map 푧↦퐴푧to each square
of 푂(see [We], Section 2.2). We denote the corresponding translation surface by 퐴⋅푆. The surface
퐴⋅푆is again an origami also denoted by 퐴⋅푂, and we can determine the gluing permutations ̃휎푎and
̃휎푏of 퐴⋅푆in terms of 퐴, 휎푎and 휎푏(cf. [SW], Section 2). Observe furthermore that the geodesics in a

Abstract: In this paper we investigate the systolic landscape of translation surfaces for ﬁxed genus and ﬁxed angles of their cone points. We furthermore study how the systoles of a translation surface relate to the systoles of its graph of saddle connections. This allows us to develop an algorithm to compute the systolic ratio of origamis in the stratum (1, 1). We compute the maximal systolic ratio of all origamis in (1, 1) with up to 67 squares. These computations support a conjecture of Judge and Parlier about the maximal systolic ratio in (1, 1).
